headline.en: Every bite you eat was once alive—plants, animals, fungi—transformed into food

universal_truth.en: We are connected to all life through what we consume; eating is participating in nature's cycles

fun_facts.en: The average meal travels over 1,500 miles from farm to plate in developed countries
Most of the world's food comes from just 12 plant species and 5 animal species
A single ear of corn has about 800 kernels—each one capable of growing a new plant

discussion_questions.en: How connected do you feel to the sources of your food?
What would change if you grew or raised some of your own food?
Why have we become so disconnected from food production?

script.en: That sandwich on your plate? The bread was wheat growing in a field. The lettuce was leaves absorbing sunlight. The meat was a living animal. Every bite you eat was alive—plants or animals transformed through farming, processing, and cooking into food.

text.en: I want to learn something new

response.en: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

script.en: Modern people rarely see food grow or animals raised. We buy packaged products with little connection to their origins. What happened between the living organism and your plate?

prompt.en: What transforms living things into food?

text.en: Farming, harvesting, processing, transportation, and preparation—a long chain from life to plate

response.en: Yes. Food systems are complex chains involving many steps and people. Each meal represents the work of farmers, processors, transporters, and cooks.

text.en: Factories process raw materials into the products we recognize as food

response.en: Processing is one step, but the chain starts much earlier—with living things growing...

script.en: The average American meal travels over 1,500 miles from farm to plate. Apples from New Zealand, fish from Norway, spices from India. Your dinner represents a global network—impressive in scale, invisible in experience.

prompt.en: What's your first impression of "Miles to Your Mouth"?

text.en: This confirms what I already knew

response.en: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

script.en: Despite thousands of edible plants, most of the world's food comes from just 12 plant species: wheat, corn, rice, potatoes, and a few others. Five animal species provide most meat. Our food system is remarkably concentrated.

prompt.en: How does this connect to what you already know?

response.en: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

text.en: I need to think about this more

response.en: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

script.en: Many foods remain alive until we eat them. Fruits and vegetables respire on your counter. Seeds in your bread could still sprout. The line between 'living thing' and 'food' is blurry—and recent.

prompt.en: What surprises you most about this?

text.en: I never thought about it this way

response.en: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

script.en: Here's today's wisdom: Eating is participating in nature's cycles. Every meal connects you to farms, ecosystems, and other living things. Understanding where food comes from changes how you think about what you eat.

prompt.en: What resonates most with you today?

response.en: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

script.en: That's Day 133. Tomorrow, we'll explore how farming changed everything. Until then, at your next meal, consider the journey each ingredient took to reach your plate.

prompt.en: Before you go—what will you take from today?

response.en: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

title.en: Food Origin Tracing - Follow the Chain

activity.en: Pick one item from your next meal and trace its origin as far as you can. Where was it grown? How far did it travel? Who touched it along the way? This simple exercise reveals the invisible systems that feed you.
